I'll review and thumb it up <@!211091239112671234> https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/pull/3101/files is the minimum requirement. <@!301186049323958275> <@!206016661470314496> couldn't the eth protocol support for the "wrapped legacy transactions" introduced earlier, not tied to a hardfork and not doing any of the other changes? Let's say that "eth/67" means that EIP-2972 style transactions are accepted on the wire, but the wrapping is dropped in the client and nothing else changes. This means the transaction pool would support these transactions today. And then when we get to the hardfork the other changes are rolled out. Not my personal preference for end-state, but getting to end-state requires more discussion it sounds like. <@!543900561460822016> Ah, you are right. I think SSZ actually is used in receipts. 😢 Not just SSZ-like. > Let's say that "eth/67" A client supporing `eth/67` _must_ support `eth/66` and `eth/65` too I understand that, btw why cannot these versions be renamed? Are some clients supporting some of them already? I assume the problem is that the handshake has a "max version accepted" field. I think no clients, maybe excepting trinity, supports `eth/66` (message-id) I wouldn't want to wind up in a scenario where clients keep putting off `eth/65`, because that one reduces the network traffic _dramatically_ But yeah, we don't want to push everyone to implement it "now now" either <@!187490121698770945> Update to 2972 to remove legacy transactions from blocks. <@!689161464829050960> <@!415548822983278593> https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/pull/2751 and https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/pull/2934 for getting rid of selfdestruct. It would be nice see if this could be done 😉 I made a comment on Zoom chat - shall we consider that we can deliver 2930 without having 2718 (like we did inside 1559( then we have time to work on 2718 I'm pretty against any transaction changes without 2718. Though, I don't actually get a vote for this sort of thing. 😛 nobody does or you do Re: Disclosure. I'm against any kind of privileged list of participants that get advanced notice of things. It reinforces centralization because it gives a competitive advantage to sufficiently large actors. Yup, he Micah get's a vote FWIW, Infura mentioned in their postmortem _they_ are also against getting advance notice: > While we have a good line of communication between our two teams, we have never expected any preferential treatment or inside access to information. No exchange, no miner, no API provider should be treated differently than a single node runner. https://blog.infura.io/infura-mainnet-outage-post-mortem-2020-11-11/amp/ Re advanced notice: It's also not crystal clear who should be on it. From a paranoid perspective: miners and downstream (alternative blockchains) might have incentives to cause chain splits on Ethereum mainnet. Rationally speaking I think that the Geth team and the EF can exercise good judgment wrt who is notified I see your point about incentives, but I would prefer if you didn't treat me as adversarial. I don't think I've done anything to warrant it 🙂 I don't treat **you** as adversarial, I actually like you very much! I just don't like the idea of creating the infrastructure and process that creates an environment for capture and competitive advantages to big actors in the system. I think those are two different points though! <@!619357961923330051> I don't see you as an adversarial, and I'm not _that_ paranoid, I was just making a point that it's not crystal clear Classic example is Infura gets on the list (big enough), QuikNode does not (not big enough). Yes, but for example, do you put ETC on the list? Are they adversarial? Do you put an "Eth2 killer" who is building off a fork of geth? Probably not, despite ETC having strong incentives to be adversarial. 😉 I did confirm to you immediately what the 'sploit was. But the basis of trust is built upon interaction. We've been having some interaction, and I've built up a trust in you, personally. That does not extend to random "downstream projects" in general, though, and I'd confide things to you that I wouldn't want to send to some official list <@!619357961923330051> I don't think there ought to be an official list. A policy that allows you to exercise good judgment re: risks/benefits of notification would be great I appreciate you confirming the issue, btw. it saved us a lot of trouble and let us act quicker it's definitely a thorny issue, particularly with downstream projects. It's hard to balance the risk of disclosure vs potential to prevent harm to downstream users Protecting stability of Ethereum mainnet is clearly the most important thing to consider. But where the risk to Ethereum is minimal, protecting users of infrastructure providers and downstream projects should be considered too anyway, we're going to take this week as an opportunity to update our own security & disclosure policies 👍 Sorry about that number change <@!211091239112671234>. Fixed now if you want to review again.

excerpts.author: axic3354
excerpts.content:
<@!301186049323958275> <@!206016661470314496> couldn't the eth protocol support for the "wrapped legacy transactions" introduced earlier, not tied to a hardfork and not doing any of the other changes?

Let's say that "eth/67" means that EIP-2972 style transactions are accepted on the wire, but the wrapping is dropped in the client and nothing else changes. This means the transaction pool would support these transactions today.

And then when we get to the hardfork the other changes are rolled out.
